content.value: Trace nested loops in execution order; distinguish rectangular from changing-bound repetition; initialize per-iteration state correctly.

A nested loop executes within the body of another loop. For each outer iteration, the inner loop runs through its own initialization, condition checks, body executions, and updates. Only after it finishes does the outer loop continue to its update. Keep a separate trace column for each index.

When the inner loop always runs the same number of times, multiply the two counts. When its bound depends on the outer index, add the different inner counts instead. Use nesting to generate coordinate pairs, repeated patterns, and later two-dimensional traversals. Reset any per-row aggregate at the beginning of each outer iteration.

The output has one star on the first line, two on the second, and three on the third. The inner body runs 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 times. col is initialized to 1 again for each new row. The println occurs after the inner loop, so it ends one row at a time.

Do not multiply 3 by 3 when the inner bound changes with row. Mixing up which variable to update can skip rows or trap the inner loop. Moving println inside the inner body would place every star on a separate line.
Predict the total number of stars if the outer bound becomes 4: 10. Then change the inner condition to col <= 4 and explain why the pattern becomes rectangular with 16 stars.
